title: Ready Queue
body:
The queue of every [[Processes|process]] that is runnable right now but is not the one on
the CPU. Being in the ready queue is what [[Process State|Ready]] means.

It is a [[Queue]] in the [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] sense: **[[FIFO]]**, enqueue at the
back, dequeue at the front. In the simplest scheduler that is the whole policy, and it is
called round robin: take the front process, run it until its time slice expires, put it on
the back, repeat. Real schedulers keep several ready queues, one per [[Process Priority]]
level, and pick from the highest non-empty one.

The distinction from the other queue:

| | [[Ready Queue]] | [[Wait Queue]] |
|---|---|---|
| Why you are here | nothing wrong, just not your turn | you asked for something unavailable |
| What gets you out | the scheduler picks you | an event fires, or `sem_post` signals you |
| How many are there | one per priority level | one per thing you can block on |
| Could you run now? | yes | no |

There is a ready queue per CPU on a multiprocessor, which is where [[Processor Affinity]]
comes from: moving a process to another CPU's ready queue throws away the [[Cache]] it had
warmed up.

A process starves when it is in the ready queue and the scheduler never gets round to it.
That is [[Starvation]], and it is exactly what [[Bounded Waiting]] rules out.
